thread.title: A Stronger Dollar Is Negative For Markets Around The World

author: George Kesarios
title: A Stronger Dollar Is Negative For Markets Around The World
text:
A Stronger Dollar Is Negative For Markets Around The World May 29, 2018 9:57 AM ET | Long/short equity, Deep Value, special situations, contrarian Summary
Dollar lending outside the U.S. has been rising for many years, and today stands at about $11.4 trillion according to the BIS.
One reason the dollar has remained strong all these years is because of dollar demand components not reflected in U.S. current account data.
If the world is deprived of dollars as a result of a lower U.S. trade deficit, this will have negative repercussions worldwide. As you all know the Fed has been rising rates for a while now, and if everybody is correct, it will raise rates an additional 3 times next year. However I think the Fed will be irresponsible in doing so. Not only will it do harm to the U.S. economy, but also to the world economy. President Trump has many times talked about the U.S. trade deficit, and that the U.S. is losing money and becoming poorer as a result. This is not exactly true. While in theory a trade and current account deficit means a country becomes poorer, the U.S. economy is the exception. This because the U.S. dollar is the world's reserve currency. Why a trade and account deficit is good for the U.S. Source As you can see from the charts above, the U.S. has a trade and current account deficit for a very long time, in fact for as long as I can remember. However, the dollar has remained strong vs most currencies in the world, and more or less on par with the euro all these years. The question is why? If the U.S. was any other country it might have had the faith of Turkey or Venezuela. The reason it does not, is because of dollar demand. But how can there be dollar demand, when there is a current account deficit? Dollar demand components that rarely anyone talks about 1) International dollar loan demand Eurodollars are bank deposit liabilities denominated in U.S. dollars but not subject to U.S. banking regulations. In other words, they are dollars in foreign banks. According to the BIS (Bank for International Settlements), International dollar denominated loans grew by 8% to $11.4 trillion in 2017, with euro loans up by 10% to €3.0 trillion . However even the BIS admits that total dollar credit might be under-reported by a whopping $14 trillion. But even if new assume that dollar lending outside the U.S. is the reported $11.4 trillion, and we assume the average interest rate on these loans is about 5% (I think it's higher), this means that about $570B in interest has to be paid on these loans every year (even assuming all loans are rolled over with no problem). This means that at the margin in the FX market, about $570B have to be found every year to service this debt. Please note this is a permanent incremental dollar demand component year in year out. Also note this figure has nothing to do with the U.S. trade deficit or current account. 2) Fuzzy trade figures Another component of FX dollar demand has to do with distorted trade data, than makes for a confusing picture. Let's take Apple ( AAPL ) as an example. Apple makes iPhones in China and then sells them all over the world. For trade purposes, Apple's products do not originate in the U.S., and therefore do not count as a trade surplus statistic for the U.S., even if Apple records this revenue figure on tis financial statements. However Apple gets paid in dollars, and its profits are also in dollars. So when an electronic retailer from some part of the world orders iPhones, it either uses its country's foreign reserves, or it exchanges is own currency for dollars in the FX market. This is another dollar demand component that has kept the U.S. dollar strong that has nothing to do with U.S. trade data. Why a strong dollar is bad for everyone Because many countries and companies around the world borrow in dollars, when interest rates in the U.S. rise, so does the cost to service this debt. So if the cost to service this dollar denominated debt rises by a lot, then we run into problems. Such was the case when Alan Greenspan tightened monetary policy begging in 1994, which led to the crisis in emerging markets in 1998. In a way, the pressure that emerging markets have felt in the past has mainly been triggered by developed economies. In addition to the higher cost of interest, when the dollar goes up, more money has to be paid in local currency, which exacerbates things further for many economies (Turkey is just one current example). Now if emerging markets get distressed, that will spill over to other more advanced economies. And if things get really bad, then we might have defaults in the emerging economy space. So as more and more dollars are required to service existing loans, the dollar rises. And every time the dollar goes up, we witness financial stress conditions across all major economies. A rising dollar, for the most part, is not good for the world economy. But a rising dollar might also spark deflation fears in the U.S., something that the Fed has been fighting since 2004 when Ben Bernanke was at the helm of the Fed. The bottom line is that a rising dollar is bad for everyone, including the U.S. Don't look at the dollar gift horse in the mouth President Trump claims the U.S. has signed very bad trade agreements all these years, and that the U.S. is getting ripped off. This is not true. This because the dollar permits the U.S. to buy stuff from other countries that it can't make, or does not want to make. It's better the buy cheap apparel from countries with cheap labor than to make it yourself, because this elevates your standard of living. Buying more with less money is a good thing. At the same time, you can pretend you have a trade deficit and let Apple make tons of money, because this money will eventually come back to the U.S. in the form of a dividend and stock repurchases, that raises Apple shares. So individuals and institutional investors become more wealthy, even if in theory you have a trade deficit (that also in theory makes you poorer). So why is the Fed so persistent on raising rates? I am not sure. The Fed knows all too well all the above arguments. It also knows that U.S. monetary policy has repercussions around the world, and is not confined to the U.S. alone. So I am not sure why it persists in raising rates higher, especially given that inflation is still not a threat. But even is inflation was a threat, it still has to take into consideration the implications of higher rates on a global scale. In my mind the risk is that the Fed might overdo it. While a 3% 10 year note is just starting to negatively impact equities - and it might take another full percentage point in fixed income yield for equity markets to take a hit - however if equity markets do take a hit, so will the economy, and so will the Fed's mandate. So I don't see why the Fed needs to raise rates further, if in the grand scheme of things they cause damage to the U.S. and world economy. Bottom line So far markets have not been too worried about interest rates. However if the Fed persists in raising rates several more times next year, then damage might be done to equities, with spillover effects into emerging markets as well as the U.S. and world economy. My hope is the Fed will not overdo it, because it understands the implications. But the same cannot be said for the U.S. administration that is on a trade crusade, supposedly to fix the wrongdoings of trade deals the U.S. signed in the past. And the problem with politics is that you cannot rely on the people involved to think rational. And this is where the risk lies. If populism and politics interrupt the flow of dollars that the world needs (via a U.S. trade deficit), then that will have negative repercussions worldwide, that will also hit the U.S. economy at some point.
